extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners learning/using ordinary differential equations (advanced undergraduate/graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Methods, theorems and solution‑construction rules for ordinary differential equations (series methods, reduction to lower order, linear equations, constant coefficients, superposition, characteristic polynomial, multiplicities, complex roots). Includes guidance on initial conditions and quadratures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series solution for ODEs (local Taylor/Maclaurin expansion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Développer la solution inconnue y en série (Taylor/Maclaurin) autour d'un point et déterminer les coefficients par substitution dans l'équation différentielle; tous les coefficients s'expriment en fonction des premiers coefficients arbitraires (pour un ordre n, en fonction des n premiers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the resulting series is convergent it defines a function satisfying the ODE in a symmetric interval around the expansion point and containing the arbitrary constants. The series may diverge (e.g., if some computed coefficient is infinite); this creates additional difficulties not pursued here. Examples: for second-order equations the coefficients are functions of the two first arbitrary coefficients; substitution and equating powers yields recurrence relations. Alternative: method of undetermined coefficients (assume a power series with unknown coefficients a_0, a_1, ... and equate coefficients).

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial value characterization of general integral
rubrics_metrics.description: L'intégrale générale d'une équation d'ordre n est une fonction y = φ(x; C1,...,Cn) contenant n constantes arbitraires qui doivent pouvoir être choisies de façon que, pour une valeur particulière x0, la fonction y et ses (n−1) premières dérivées prennent des valeurs arbitraires données.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the characterization of the general solution: the arbitrary constants are determined by prescribing the values of y, y', ..., y^{(n-1)} at a given point (initial conditions). Examples are given for n=1,2,...

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular integrals vs singular integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: Les intégrales particulières sont obtenues en donnant des valeurs numériques aux constantes arbitraires de l'intégrale générale; il peut exister d'autres solutions, appelées intégrales singulières.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between particular solutions obtained by specializing constants and genuinely singular solutions that are not obtainable by specializing the general integral. Note: later, for linear equations it is stated that no singular integrals exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to first order when the equation lacks y (no explicit y)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the differential equation of second order is of the form F(x,y',y'')=0 (y missing), take y' as the auxiliary unknown and reduce to a first‑order equation in y'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve the first-order equation f(x,y')=0 to obtain y' = φ(x,C); then integrate (quadrature) to obtain y(x) with the second arbitrary constant appearing after integration. Example: 3x y' = y^2 + 2x^2 — set z = y' and solve the resulting homogeneous first‑order equation, separate variables, integrate using partial fractions, then integrate y' to find y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to first order when the equation lacks x (autonomous in x)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the differential equation is of the form F(y,y',y'')=0 (x missing), set v = y' and transform to an equation between v and y: dv/dx = (dv/dy)(dy/dx) etc., obtaining a first‑order equation between v and y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate to get v = φ(y,C) (or express y' in terms of y), then use dy/dx = v(y) to obtain dx (or x) by quadrature. Often convenient to express x and y parametrically in terms of the auxiliary variable y'. Examples: motion under a force depending only on position and velocity; elastic plane curve where curvature depends on y leads to an equation not containing x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two canonical reduction cases for second-order ODEs
rubrics_metrics.description: Two standard cases reduce integration of a second order ODE to integrating a first order ODE followed by a quadrature: (1) the equation does not contain y, (2) the equation does not contain x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reduced first‑order equation falls into a known integrable type, one can complete the integration. The section gives procedures and worked examples for both cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: treating y' as new unknown and quadrature
rubrics_metrics.description: When reducing to first order one often sets the derivative as a new unknown and after solving the first‑order equation one recovers y by a quadrature (integration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quadrature may require algebraic manipulation such as decomposition into partial fractions; provide constants of integration at each step. Examples show explicit computation of integrals and algebraic substitutions to evaluate the quadrature.

rubrics_metrics.name: General reducibility criterion to first order for order n
rubrics_metrics.description: An equation of order n is reducible to first order when it contains neither the unknown function nor its derivatives of orders 1,2,...,(n−2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In that case the equation can be written F(x,y^{(n−1)})=0 and reduced to a first‑order equation in the highest derivative; integrating successively (n−1) times and adding arbitrary constants yields y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of linear ODE (order n)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ODE of order n is linear when it is linear in the unknown function and its derivatives. It has the form: a_n(x) y^{(n)} + a_{n-1}(x) y^{(n-1)} + ... + a_0(x) y = X(x) (X is the second member).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When X=0 the equation is linear homogeneous (sans deuxième membre). Study of linear equations is fundamental for physics and mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity properties / superposition principle
rubrics_metrics.description: For the linear differential operator Φ(y): Φ(C u) = C Φ(u) and Φ(u+v) = Φ(u) + Φ(v); hence linear combinations of solutions of the homogeneous equation are also solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem I and II show that if y1,...,yn are solutions of the homogeneous equation, then any linear combination with constant coefficients is also a solution. Use this to build general solution once a fundamental set is known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear independence / distinctness of solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two solutions are distinct if one is not a constant multiple of the other; more generally p solutions are distinct (linearly independent) if none is a constant linear combination of the previous ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notion is used to count the dimension of the solution space: for an order n homogeneous linear equation the maximum number of linearly independent solutions is n. Examples: e^x, sin x, cos x are independent; cos 2x, cos x, sin 2x are not all independent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of general solution from n independent solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: If n linearly independent solutions y1,...,yn of a homogeneous linear equation of order n are known, the general integral is y = C1 y1 + C2 y2 + ... + Cn yn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This general integral contains n arbitrary constants which are determined by initial conditions at a point; if the known solutions were not independent the expression would contain fewer than n constants. Theorem III and follow-ups justify this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear homogeneous ODEs have no singular integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear differential equation has no singular integrals: all solutions are given by the general integral constructed from n independent solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated (without long proof) as a property of linear equations; contrasts with nonlinear equations which may admit singular integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order lowering (reduction) when a solution is known
rubrics_metrics.description: If one solution y0 of a linear homogeneous ODE is known, one can reduce the order by substituting y = y0 * Y (or other change) to derive an equation of order n−1 for Y, thus 'abaisser l'ordre' by one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: set y = y0 * Y, compute derivatives, substitute into the ODE; the coefficient of Y vanishes leading to an equation in Y of one less order. Repeating the process when further solutions are known reduces order further. After solving for Y, recover y by quadratures (integration). A worked example is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for constant coefficient linear homogeneous ODEs: characteristic polynomial
rubrics_metrics.description: For a linear homogeneous ODE with constant coefficients, look for solutions y = e^{r x}. Substitution yields a polynomial Φ(r) (characteristic polynomial); roots r_i produce elementary solutions e^{r_i x}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all roots are distinct, general solution is sum C_i e^{r_i x}. If roots are repeated or complex, see multiplicity and complex root rules below. Examples and computations of Φ(r) given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of characteristic roots: x^k e^{r x} factors
rubrics_metrics.description: If r is a root of multiplicity p of the characteristic polynomial, then the equation admits p independent solutions: e^{r x}, x e^{r x}, x^2 e^{r x}, ..., x^{p-1} e^{r x}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration uses differentiating parameter families e^{r x} w.r.t. r and identities showing successive derivatives vanish when r is multiple root. Examples: triple root gives solutions e^{x}, x e^{x}, x^2 e^{x}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex roots lead to real sine/cosine solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: If characteristic roots are complex (conjugate pair α ± iβ), the corresponding real independent solutions are e^{α x} cos(β x) and e^{α x} sin(β x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Euler's identity e^{(α+iβ)x} = e^{α x}(cos βx + i sin βx) and choose complex conjugate constants so that the final solution is real. Examples show conversion from complex exponential basis to real trigonometric basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series method recurrence: coefficients determined by recurrence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting a power series into the ODE and equating coefficients of like powers yields a recurrence relation among coefficients; for second order this relates a_{n+2} to previous coefficients, giving all coefficients in terms of the first two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for y'' + y = 0 the recurrence produces cos x and sin x series. The text shows how to group terms multiplying the arbitrary initial coefficients to identify closed form solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical remarks about choosing variables to integrate first-order reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: When integrating the reduced first-order equation it may be convenient to express x as a function of y' (or vice versa) and represent the general integral implicitly as X(y',C). Then use dy/dx relations to obtain y by quadrature or to express x and y parametrically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equations (12),(13),(17),(18) illustrate expressing x and y in terms of auxiliary variable y' and eliminating it to obtain the general solution. Use appropriate variable choices to simplify quadratures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadrature and algebraic techniques required in integrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Integration steps after reduction often reduce to evaluating explicit integrals (quadratures) which may require algebraic manipulations: substitution, partial fraction decomposition, change of variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked examples demonstrate partial fraction decomposition and substitutions (e.g., u-substitutions) to compute the quadratures explicitly; constants of integration appear at each integration step.
